claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
The baseline alloy has a density of approximately 12.5 g/cm³.
The baseline alloy is brittle at room temperature because of limited dislocation mobility and easy cleavage fracture.
Adding 1.5 at.% Si will precipitate a Laves phase with a C14 or C15 structure.
The Si-induced Laves phase will form a continuous reticulated network at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200°C for 24 hours and water quenching will stabilize the proposed secondary phase.
The proposed secondary phase is an Hf/Mo/Ta/Zr-rich silicide Laves phase.
The reticulated Laves-phase network will deflect cracks from straight cleavage paths.
The network will promote crack-tip blunting through localized plasticity in the adjacent BCC matrix.
The Laves-phase network will provide load-transfer strengthening.
The Si-alloyed sample will show a 15–25% increase in compressive plastic strain to failure relative to the baseline.
The Si-alloyed sample will show a yield-strength increase of less than 5%.
Adding Si will increase density by approximately 0.3–0.5%.
The predicted density increase arises from Si having a higher atomic mass than the average matrix composition and from denser packing of the Laves phase.
The mechanism holds only below an approximately 2.5 at.% Si peritectic limit for massive Laves-phase formation.
Exceeding approximately 2.5 at.% Si may produce coarse continuous brittle networks and catastrophic embrittlement.
At temperatures above 0.5 Tm, the Laves phase may coarsen or dissolve and alter the mechanism.
Room-temperature compression is to be performed at 298 K and a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
An increase in ductility without secondary-phase formation would falsify the proposed phase-network mechanism in favor of a solid-solution explanation.
Formation of the secondary phase accompanied by reduced ductility would falsify its proposed role as a beneficial crack-deflection network.
